title: Chapter XLI

teacherSummary.text: Lydia is invited to Brighton by Mrs. Forster. Elizabeth warns her father of the danger; Mr. Bennet lets Lydia go to keep peace. Elizabeth sees Wickham again and hints she knows the truth.

vocabulary.context: If you, my dear father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “exuberant”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ant (Latin -ans, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of vexing, or the state of being vexed
vocabulary.context: It was not in her nature, however, to increase her vexations, by dwelling on them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “vexation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Having a stomach that is easily or nauseated
vocabulary.context: Such squeamish youths as cannot bear to be connected with a little absurdity, are not worth a regret.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “squeamish”: ami (Latin amare, "to love"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: “And pray may I ask?” but checking himself, he added in a gayer tone, “Is it in address that he improves?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “improve”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To perform a work or labor
vocabulary.context: His fear of her, has always operated, I know, when they were together; and a good deal is to be imputed to his wish of forwarding the match with Miss de Bourgh, which I am certain he has very much at heart.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “operate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state of being the same, identity
vocabulary.context: She had even learnt to detect, in the very gentleness which had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness to disgust and weary.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sameness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn-house.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “resound”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To refer to something indirectly or by suggestion
vocabulary.context: I only fear that the sort of cautiousness, to which you, I imagine, have been alluding, is merely adopted on his visits to his aunt, of whose good opinion and judgment he stands much in awe.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “allude”: -ude (Latin -udo, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: This invaluable friend was a very young woman, and very lately married.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “invaluable”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: In his present behaviour to herself, moreover, she had a fresh source of displeasure, for the inclination he soon testified of renewing those attentions which had marked the early part of their acquaintance, could only serve, after what had since passed, to provoke her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “renew”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Chaperones were expected to protect young women's reputations.

significance: Mr. Bennet's indifference is a serious moral failing that leads to crisis.
discussionQuestions: Is Mr. Bennet responsible for what happens next?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLI,” how does Austen show parental failure? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLI develops the idea of parental failure. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLI to complicate the reader's understanding of parental failure. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of parental failure responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of parental failure. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn-house. Elizabeth tried to be diverted by them; but all sense of pleasure was lost in shame. She felt anew the justice of Mr. Darcy’s objections; and never had she before been so much disposed to pardon his interference in the views of his friend.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLI”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn-house. Elizabeth tried to be diverted by them; but all sense of pleasure was lost in shame. She felt anew the justice of Mr. Darcy’s objections; and never had she before been so much disposed to pardon his interference in the views of his friend.

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is Mr. Bennet responsible for what happens next? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are exuberant, vexations, squeamish, improves, operated. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “If you, my dear father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment.” Webster's says: Characterized by abundance or superabundance. Now the word history: “exuberant”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ant (Latin -ans, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “vexation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “squeamish”: ami (Latin amare, "to love"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Chaperones were expected to protect young women's reputations. Why does this chapter matter? Mr. Bennet's indifference is a serious moral failing that leads to crisis. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to parental failure.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Foreshadowing.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn-house. Elizabeth tried to be diverted by them; but all sense of pleasure was lost in shame. She felt anew the justice of Mr. Darcy’s objections; and never had she before been so much disposed to pardon his interference in the views of his friend.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Foreshadowing: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLI,” how does Austen show parental failure? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about parental failure, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes parental failure. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
